claim: Set1 is the catalytic subunit of the Set1C/COMPASS complex responsible for histone H3K4 methylation (H3K4me) in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: Here, we show that Set1, the catalytic subunit of the highly conserved Set1C/COMPASS complex responsible for histone H3K4 methylation (H3K4me), behaves as a repressor of the transcriptome largely independent of Set1C and H3K4me in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by the study's experimental design and results.

claim: Set1 behaves as a repressor of the transcriptome largely independent of Set1C and H3K4me in S. pombe.
source: Here, we show that Set1, the catalytic subunit of the highly conserved Set1C/COMPASS complex responsible for histone H3K4 methylation (H3K4me), behaves as a repressor of the transcriptome largely independent of Set1C and H3K4me in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome profiling data showing that loss of set1 affects nearly 1000 probes while H3K4me mutants affect only ~100 probes (Figure 1A).

claim: Set1 is enriched at both highly expressed and repressed loci.
source: Intriguingly, while Set1 is enriched at highly expressed and repressed loci, Set1 binding levels do not generally correlate with the levels of transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-chip data showing Set1 localization at active genes like act1 and repressed genes like ste11 (Figure 2A, B).

claim: Set1 binding levels do not generally correlate with the levels of transcription.
source: Intriguingly, while Set1 is enriched at highly expressed and repressed loci, Set1 binding levels do not generally correlate with the levels of transcription.
evidence: This is shown by ranking Set1-bound genes by expression level, which reveals no linear correlation between Set1 binding and transcript abundance (Figure 2C).

claim: Set1 is recruited by the ATF/CREB homolog Atf1 to heterochromatic loci and promoters of stress-response genes.
source: We show that Set1 is recruited by the ATF/CREB homolog Atf1 to heterochromatic loci and promoters of stress-response genes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-chip data showing colocalization of Atf1 and Set1 at centromeres, rDNA, and ste11 (Figure 3A-C), and reduced Set1 enrichment in atf1Δ cells (Figure 3D).

claim: Set1 coordinates with the class II histone deacetylase Clr3 in heterochromatin assembly at prominent chromosomal landmarks.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that Set1 coordinates with the class II histone deacetylase Clr3 in heterochromatin assembly at prominent chromosomal landmarks and repression of the transcriptome that includes Tf2 retrotransposons, noncoding RNAs, and regulators of development and stress-responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by synthetic growth defects in set1Δ clr3Δ double mutants (Figure 4A), synergistic derepression of pericentromeric repeats (Figure 4C), and dramatic reduction of H3K9me2 in the double mutant (Figure 4D, E).

claim: Set1 and Clr3 coordinate in repression of Tf2 retrotransposons, noncoding RNAs, and regulators of development and stress-responses.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that Set1 coordinates with the class II histone deacetylase Clr3 in heterochromatin assembly at prominent chromosomal landmarks and repression of the transcriptome that includes Tf2 retrotransposons, noncoding RNAs, and regulators of development and stress-responses.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis showing that set1Δ clr3Δ double mutants have nearly 2900 differentially expressed probes, including Tf2s and developmental genes (Figure 5A, C).

claim: Loss of set1 resulted in significant derepression of nearly 1000 of ~42,000 tiling microarray probes.
source: Whereas loss of set1 resulted in significant derepression of nearly 1000 of ∼42,000 tiling microarray probes (average log2 fold-change vs wild-type >1.5, p < 0.05), H3K4me null mutants H3K4R (histone H3 lysine 4 substituted with arginine) or set1FH3K4me− (H3K4me abolished by Set1 C-terminal FLAG epitope insertion) (Lorenz et al., 2012; Mikheyeva et al., 2014) affected ∼100 probes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the microarray data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: H3K4me null mutants H3K4R or set1FH3K4me− affected approximately 100 probes.
source: Whereas loss of set1 resulted in significant derepression of nearly 1000 of ∼42,000 tiling microarray probes (average log2 fold-change vs wild-type >1.5, p < 0.05), H3K4me null mutants H3K4R (histone H3 lysine 4 substituted with arginine) or set1FH3K4me− (H3K4me abolished by Set1 C-terminal FLAG epitope insertion) (Lorenz et al., 2012; Mikheyeva et al., 2014) affected ∼100 probes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the microarray data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The Set1C complex includes seven other subunits in addition to Set1.
source: Set1 is the catalytic engine of the Set1C complex that includes seven other subunits (Roguev et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation to Roguev et al., 2003.

claim: Except for Shg1, Set1 and six S. pombe subunits (Swd1, Swd2, Swd3, Spp1, Ash2, Sdc1) have orthologs in S. cerevisiae and humans.
source: Except for Shg1, Set1 and six S. pombe subunits (Swd1, Swd2, Swd3, Spp1, Ash2, Sdc1) have orthologs in S. cerevisiae and humans (Roguev et al., 2003; Shevchenko et al., 2008; Shilatifard, 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Loss of individual Set1C complex subunits affects differentially the levels and states of H3K4me in S. pombe.
source: Loss of individual Set1C complex subunits affects differentially the levels and states of H3K4me in S. pombe (Roguev et al., 2003; Mikheyeva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Loss of ash2 primarily resulted in increased sense transcription.
source: loss of ash2 primarily resulted in increased sense transcription, and loss of shg1, spp1, or swd3 predominantly affected intergenic transcripts.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B which displays the percentage of probes by strand/location.

claim: Loss of shg1, spp1, or swd3 predominantly affected intergenic transcripts.
source: loss of ash2 primarily resulted in increased sense transcription, and loss of shg1, spp1, or swd3 predominantly affected intergenic transcripts.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B which displays the percentage of probes by strand/location.

claim: The profile of set1Δ contains a large set of upregulated transcripts including Tf2 retrotransposons, pericentromeric repeats, and long noncoding RNAs.
source: The profile of set1Δ forms its own distinct group, containing a large set of upregulated transcripts including Tf2 retrotransposons, pericentromeric repeats, and long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) that were little affected in the other Set1C and H3K4me mutants (Figure 1C, lower panel; Figure 1—source data 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the hierarchical clustering analysis in Figure 1C.

claim: H3K4me is enriched at transcriptionally active loci.
source: While H3K4me is known to be enriched at transcriptionally active loci (Cam et al., 2005; Pokholok et al., 2005), we consistently observed transcriptional derepression in the set1Δ mutant at non-active, stress-response genes or heterochromatic repeats.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Set1 is enriched at sites that correspond to highly active Pol II promoters, including those of the housekeeping gene act1 and the ribosomal protein rps102.
source: Consistent with its documented recruitment to active Pol II genes (Ng et al., 2003), Set1 is enriched at sites that correspond to highly active Pol II promoters, including those of the housekeeping gene act1 and the ribosomal protein rps102 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figure 2A.

claim: Noticeable Set1 binding was detected at the promoters of lowly expressed genes (e.g., scr1) and repressed developmental genes (e.g., ste11) despite little enrichment of Pol II.
source: Surprisingly, despite little enrichment of Pol II at certain lowly expressed genes (e.g., scr1) and repressed developmental genes (e.g., ste11), noticeable Set1 binding was detected at the promoters of these genes (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 80% of promoter regions enriched for Set1 corresponded to actively transcribed genes.
source: While transcript abundance generally correlated with Pol II occupancy levels (Figure 2C, middle panel) and 80% of promoter regions enriched for Set1 corresponded to actively transcribed genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), transcript abundance or Pol II occupancy levels did not linearly correlate with the levels of Set1 binding (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Highly expressed genes occupied by Set1 were enriched with GO terms associated with rapid exponential growth (ribosome, translation, glycolysis).
source: Whereas highly expressed genes occupied by Set1 were enriched with expected GO terms associated with rapid exponential growth (ribosome, translation, glycolysis), Set1-bound genes with low abundance transcripts (excluding heterochromatic noncoding RNAs due to limited GO annotation) were enriched for terms related to stress response, cell wall and membrane-bound protein biogenesis, and Pol II transcription factor function (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown by GO analysis in Figure 2D and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Set1-bound genes with low abundance transcripts were enriched for GO terms related to stress response, cell wall and membrane-bound protein biogenesis, and Pol II transcription factor function.
source: Whereas highly expressed genes occupied by Set1 were enriched with expected GO terms associated with rapid exponential growth (ribosome, translation, glycolysis), Set1-bound genes with low abundance transcripts (excluding heterochromatic noncoding RNAs due to limited GO annotation) were enriched for terms related to stress response, cell wall and membrane-bound protein biogenesis, and Pol II transcription factor function (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown by GO analysis in Figure 2D and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Atf1 localizes to its targets before their activation.
source: In addition to localizing to its targets before their activation (Eshaghi et al., 2010), which is important for subsequent proper response to environmental stresses (Chen et al., 2003), Atf1 contributes to heterochromatic silencing at the silent mating-type locus (Jia et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Atf1 contributes to heterochromatic silencing at the silent mating-type locus.
source: In addition to localizing to its targets before their activation (Eshaghi et al., 2010), which is important for subsequent proper response to environmental stresses (Chen et al., 2003), Atf1 contributes to heterochromatic silencing at the silent mating-type locus (Jia et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation to Jia et al., 2004.

claim: Atf1 and Set1 colocalize at centromeric tRNA clusters flanking the euchromatin/heterochromatin boundaries of centromere II and the inner imr repeats of the central core.
source: We observed colocalization of Atf1 and Set1 at centromeric tRNA clusters flanking the euchromatin/heterochromatin boundaries of centromere II and the inner imr repeats of the central core (Figure 3A, upper panel).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figure 3A.

claim: Similar colocalization patterns of Atf1 and Set1 were detected at centromeres I and III.
source: Similar colocalization patterns were detected at centromeres I and III (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, upper panels).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Atf1 and Set1 colocalize at the intergenic region of the rDNA and the promoter of the developmental regulator ste11.
source: We also detected colocalization of Atf1 and Set1 at the intergenic region of the rDNA and the promoter of the developmental regulator ste11 (Figure 3B,C, upper panel; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figures 3B, 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In wild-type cells, H3K4me3 signals could be detected throughout the centromere central cores and the rDNA array but were little enriched at the ste11 promoter.
source: In wild-type cells, H3K4me3 signals could be detected throughout the centromere central cores and the rDNA array but were little enriched at the ste11 promoter (Figure 3A,B, C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, bottom panels).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figures 3A, 3B, 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of atf1 resulted in a sizeable reduction of H3K4me3 levels throughout the central cores and rDNA array.
source: Loss of atf1 resulted in a sizeable reduction of H3K4me3 levels throughout the central cores and rDNA array.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data comparing wild-type and atf1Δ cells in Figures 3A, 3B, 3C.

claim: Set1 enrichment at centromere central cores, rDNA array, and ste11 was reduced in atf1Δ cells.
source: We found that Set1 enrichment at these loci, including the ste11 gene, was reduced in atf1Δ cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP data in Figure 3D.

claim: At ste11, Atf1 and Set1 appear to act primarily in parallel pathways to keep ste11 expression repressed.
source: At ste11, Atf1 and Set1 appear to act primarily in parallel pathways to keep ste11 expression repressed, as appreciable upregulation of ste11 expression was seen only in mutants deficient for both atf1 and set1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by expression analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: More than one-third of Atf1 and Set1 bound loci are co-occupied by both proteins (p < 0.001).
source: Comparing Atf1 and Set1 localization at the genome scale revealed 217 and 261 distinct bound loci for Atf1 or Set1, respectively, with more than one-third co-occupied by both proteins (p < 0.001, Fisher's exact test) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by genome-wide ChIP-chip analysis in Figure 3E.

claim: The class II HDAC Clr3 contributes to transcriptional silencing of heterochromatin.
source: The class II HDAC Clr3 has been shown to contribute to transcriptional silencing of heterochromatin (Grewal et al., 1998; Yamada et al., 2005) Tf2 retrotransposons (Hansen et al., 2005; Cam et al., 2008), and stress-response genes (Lorenz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Clr3 contributes to transcriptional silencing of Tf2 retrotransposons.
source: The class II HDAC Clr3 has been shown to contribute to transcriptional silencing of heterochromatin (Grewal et al., 1998; Yamada et al., 2005) Tf2 retrotransposons (Hansen et al., 2005; Cam et al., 2008), and stress-response genes (Lorenz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Clr3 contributes to transcriptional silencing of stress-response genes.
source: The class II HDAC Clr3 has been shown to contribute to transcriptional silencing of heterochromatin (Grewal et al., 1998; Yamada et al., 2005) Tf2 retrotransposons (Hansen et al., 2005; Cam et al., 2008), and stress-response genes (Lorenz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: A double mutant set1Δ clr3Δ strain exhibited a significant synthetic slow-growth phenotype and sensitivity to the tubulin inhibitor thiabendazole.
source: We observed that in contrast to wild-type or single set1Δ or clr3Δ mutant strains, a double mutant set1Δ clr3Δ strain exhibited a significant synthetic slow-growth phenotype and sensitivity to the tubulin inhibitor thiabendazole (Figure 4A), suggesting defects in chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is shown by serial dilution analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: The set1FH3K4me− clr3Δ double mutant exhibited only slight defects compared to set1Δ clr3Δ.
source: Importantly, the set1FH3K4me− clr3Δ double mutant, in which set1 has no H3K4me activity, exhibited only slight defects.
evidence: This is shown by serial dilution analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: Additional derepression of a pericentromeric reporter gene was observed in mutants deficient for both set1 and clr3.
source: Derepression of a reporter gene inserted within the pericentromeric repeats has been observed in mutants deficient for either set1 (Kanoh et al., 2003) or clr3 (Grewal et al., 1998). We observed additional derepression of the reporter gene in mutants deficient for both set1 and clr3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by 5-FOA assay in Figure 4B.

claim: In the set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant, the increase in pericentromeric transcript levels was synergistic and occurred throughout the entire pericentromeric region.
source: Modest increases in transcript levels were found on both strands associated with the pericentromeric dg and dh repeats in single set1Δ and clr3Δ mutants. However, in the set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant, the increase was not only synergistic but occurred throughout the entire pericentromeric region (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by tiling microarray data in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of clr3 resulted in increased levels of H3K9me2 and Pol II and a decrease in Swi6 enrichment at pericentromeric dg repeats.
source: Similar to previous observations (Yamada et al., 2005), the loss of clr3 resulted in increased levels of H3K9me2 and Pol II and a decrease in Swi6 enrichment (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of set1 resulted in a slight increase of Pol II localization and did not diminish H3K9me2 and Swi6 levels at the dg repeats.
source: Loss of set1 resulted in a slight increase of Pol II localization (Xhemalce and Kouzarides, 2010) and did not diminish H3K9me2 and Swi6 levels at the dg repeats.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a dramatic reduction in the levels of H3K9me2 and Swi6 accompanied by further increase of Pol II occupancy in the set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant.
source: In contrast, there was a dramatic reduction in the levels of H3K9me2 and Swi6 accompanied by further increase of Pol II occupancy in the double mutant lacking both set1 and clr3.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3K9me2 levels in set1Δ clr3Δ mutant were reduced across the entire pericentromeric region.
source: We extended our analysis of H3K9me2 genome-wide and found that H3K9me2 levels in set1Δ clr3Δ mutant were reduced across the entire pericentromeric region (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figure 4E.

claim: H3K9me2 defects in the set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant were seen at other centromeres and heterochromatin domains, including the silent mating type region and subtelomeres.
source: H3K9me2 defects in the double mutant were seen at other centromeres and heterochromatin domains, including the silent mating type region and subtelomeres (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of clr3 or set1 resulted in an increase of siRNAs.
source: We found that whereas loss of clr3 or set1 resulted in an increase of siRNAs (Sugiyama et al., 2007), the level of siRNAs was dramatically reduced in the double mutant (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown by northern blot analysis in Figure 4F.

claim: The level of siRNAs was dramatically reduced in the set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant.
source: We found that whereas loss of clr3 or set1 resulted in an increase of siRNAs (Sugiyama et al., 2007), the level of siRNAs was dramatically reduced in the double mutant (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown by northern blot analysis in Figure 4F.

claim: Loss of clr3 resulted in 792 probes changing significantly in comparison with wild-type, with approximately equal numbers corresponding to upregulated and downregulated transcripts.
source: While the majority of the differentially expressed probes in the set1Δ mutant corresponded to increased expression, loss of clr3 resulted in 792 probes changing significantly in comparison with wild-type, with approximately equal numbers corresponding to upregulated and downregulated transcripts (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by microarray data in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells lacking both set1 and clr3 displayed differential expression of nearly 2900 probes, 2343 of which were upregulated.
source: Intriguingly, cells lacking both set1 and clr3 displayed differential expression of nearly 2900 probes, 2343 of which were upregulated.
evidence: This is shown by microarray data in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of H3K4me in a clr3 null background (set1FH3K4me− clr3Δ) did not produce such a drastic change to the transcriptome compared with set1Δ clr3Δ.
source: Loss of H3K4me in a clr3 null background (set1FH3K4me− clr3Δ) did not produce such a drastic change to the transcriptome compared with set1Δ clr3Δ, but only reduced the proportion of downregulated transcripts seen in the single clr3Δ mutant.
evidence: This is shown by microarray data in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of both set1 and clr3 resulted in significant expression changes within protein-coding gene regions for a large subset of genes displaying negligible change in individual set1 or clr3 mutants.
source: Most notably, loss of both set1 and clr3 resulted in significant expression changes within protein-coding gene regions for a large subset of genes displaying negligible change in individual set1 or clr3 mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by hierarchical clustering in Figure 5C.

claim: Upregulated transcripts in set1Δ clr3Δ include well-characterized developmental and stress-response regulatory proteins that include fbp1, mei2 and ste11.
source: Upregulated transcripts include well-characterized developmental and stress-response regulatory proteins that include fbp1, mei2 and ste11 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by expression analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Most of the upregulated transcripts in set1Δ clr3Δ are associated with stress-response processes that include the Tor2-Mei2-Ste11 pathways.
source: Gene ontology analysis suggested that most of the upregulated transcripts in set1Δ clr3Δ are associated with stress-response processes that include the Tor2-Mei2-Ste11 pathways (Figure 5D; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown by GO analysis in Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: The set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant exhibited considerable meiotic defects compared with wild-type or single mutant strains.
source: In this regard, we noted that compared with wild-type or single mutant strains, the set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant exhibited considerable meiotic defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by iodine staining of meiotic products in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Acetylation of histones by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) is generally associated with gene activation.
source: Whereas acetylation of histones by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) is generally associated with gene activation (Rando and Chang, 2009), deacetylation of histones by histone deacetylases (HDACs) tends to correlate with gene repression (Yang and Seto, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Deacetylation of histones by histone deacetylases (HDACs) tends to correlate with gene repression.
source: Whereas acetylation of histones by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) is generally associated with gene activation (Rando and Chang, 2009), deacetylation of histones by histone deacetylases (HDACs) tends to correlate with gene repression (Yang and Seto, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Methylation at lysine 4 of histone H3 (H3K4me) and at lysine 9 (H3K9me) distinguishes euchromatin and heterochromatin, respectively.
source: Methylation at lysine 4 of histone H3 (H3K4me) and at lysine 9 (H3K9me) distinguishes euchromatin and heterochromatin, respectively (Litt et al., 2001; Noma et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Islands of H3K9me are transiently assembled within euchromatin at certain meiotic genes and the 3′ ends of convergent genes in S. pombe.
source: However, studies from the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe and other systems show that the euchromatic and heterochromatic landscapes are somewhat fluid, with islands of H3K9me transiently assembled within euchromatin at certain meiotic genes and the 3′ ends of convergent genes (Cam et al., 2005; Huisinga et al., 2006; Gullerova and Proudfoot, 2008; Zofall et al., 2012; Tashiro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: The RNA interference (RNAi) and exosome machineries, certain HATs and an active RNA polymerase II (Pol II) contribute directly to the assembly of heterochromatin.
source: Conversely, the RNA interference (RNAi) and exosome machineries, certain HATs and an active RNA polymerase II (Pol II) have been documented to contribute directly to the assembly of heterochromatin (Volpe et al., 2002; Djupedal et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2005; Buhler et al., 2007; Xhemalce and Kouzarides, 2010; Reyes-Turcu et al., 2011; Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae homolog of Set1 (KMT2) responsible for H3K4 methylation has been implicated in transcriptional silencing at a number of genetic elements.
source: In particular, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae homolog of Set1 (KMT2) responsible for H3K4 methylation (H3K4me) has been implicated in transcriptional silencing at a number of genetic elements (Nislow et al., 1997; Krogan et al., 2002; Berretta et al., 2008; Camblong et al., 2009; Kim and Buratowski, 2009; van Dijk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: Set1C subunits have been shown to be recruited to active Pol II genes and provide the H3K4me signature for the gene-rich euchromatin.
source: Set1C subunits have been shown to be recruited to active Pol II genes and provide the H3K4me signature for the gene-rich euchromatin (Krogan et al., 2003; Ng et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 are enriched at gene promoters and gene bodies, respectively.
source: The three forms of H3K4me have different distributions, with H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 enriched at gene promoters and gene bodies, respectively (Cam et al., 2005; Pokholok et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: H3K4me1 is enriched at the 3′ end of Pol II genes in budding yeast and at enhancers in mammals.
source: H3K4me1 is enriched at the 3′ end of Pol II genes in budding yeast and at enhancers in mammals (Pokholok et al., 2005; Heintzman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: The repressor function of Set1C in S. cerevisiae is ascribed to H3K4me2 and/or H3K4me3.
source: Gene expression profiling analyses ascribe the repressor function of Set1C to H3K4me2 and/or H3K4me3 (Margaritis et al., 2012; Weiner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: S. pombe Set1 has a role in the transcriptional repression and genome organization of long terminal repeat Tf2 retrotransposons and heterochromatic repeats that are dependent and independent of the Set1C complex and H3K4 methylation.
source: We have recently discovered a role for the S. pombe Set1 in the transcriptional repression and genome organization of long terminal repeat Tf2 retrotransposons and heterochromatic repeats that are dependent and independent of the Set1C complex and H3K4 methylation (Lorenz et al., 2012; Mikheyeva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Loss of set1 or any of the other four core Set1C subunits (Swd1, Swd3, Bre2/Ash2, Sdc1) produces comparable expression profiles in S. cerevisiae.
source: Recent transcriptome studies of chromatin mutants in S. cerevisiae reveal that loss of set1 or any of the other four core Set1C subunits (Swd1, Swd3, Bre2/Ash2, Sdc1) produces comparable expression profiles (Margaritis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation.

claim: Loss of set1 in S. cerevisiae has only a modest effect on the transcriptome, mainly towards derepression that could fully be accounted by the loss of H3K4me.
source: Furthermore, loss of set1 has only a modest effect on the transcriptome, mainly towards derepression that could fully be accounted by the loss of H3K4me (Margaritis et al., 2012; Weiner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: S. pombe Set1 might mediate its repressive nonH3K4me function via a distinct form of Set1 different from the form associated with the canonical Set1C complex.
source: Interestingly, S. pombe Set1 has been reported as a component of at least two complexes: a large ∼1 MDa complex similar in size to that of S. cerevisiae Set1C and a smaller complex (∼800 kDa) containing a shorter version of Set1 (Roguev et al., 2003). Thus, Set1 might mediate its repressive nonH3K4me function via a distinct form of Set1 different from the form associated with the canonical Set1C complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Set1 exists in multiple complexes and has H3K4me-independent functions.

claim: Co-occupancy of Set1 and Atf1 at the promoters of certain developmental and stress-response regulators helps keep these genes in a poised transcriptional off-state.
source: It is likely that co-occupancy of Set1 and Atf1 at the promoters of certain developmental and stress-response regulators not only helps keep these genes in a poised transcriptional off-state, but might also contribute to their rapid transcriptional activation in response to proper developmental or environmental stress signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Set1 and Atf1 colocalize at stress-response genes and both contribute to their repression.

claim: Co-occupancy of Set1 and Atf1 at the promoters of certain developmental and stress-response regulators might contribute to their rapid transcriptional activation in response to proper developmental or environmental stress signals.
source: It is likely that co-occupancy of Set1 and Atf1 at the promoters of certain developmental and stress-response regulators not only helps keep these genes in a poised transcriptional off-state, but might also contribute to their rapid transcriptional activation in response to proper developmental or environmental stress signals.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known role of Atf1 in stress response and the observation of Set1/Atf1 colocalization.

claim: Pol II activity is required for transcriptional silencing and heterochromatin assembly at pericentromeric repeats.
source: Pol II activity is known to be required for transcriptional silencing and heterochromatin assembly at pericentromeric repeats (Djupedal et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Components of the Mediator complex contribute to heterochromatin formation.
source: Other factors associated with active Pol II transcription including components of the Mediator complex have also been shown to contribute to heterochromatin formation (Oya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation.

claim: Set1 represses transcription on both the forward and reverse strands of the pericentromeric repeats.
source: Set1 represses transcription on both the forward and reverse strands of the pericentromeric repeats and cooperates with Clr3 to assemble H3K9me-associated heterochromatin.
evidence: This is shown by bidirectional transcription analysis in Figure 4C.

claim: The heterochromatic activity of Set1 appears to be independent of its canonical H3K4me function associated with the Set1C complex.
source: Importantly, this heterochromatic activity of Set1 appears to be independent of its canonical H3K4me function associated with the Set1C complex, consistent with previous observations for the general lack of H3K4me within H3K9me heterochromatin (Noma et al., 2001; Cam et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that set1FH3K4me− clr3Δ double mutant shows only slight defects compared to set1Δ clr3Δ, and supported by citations.

claim: Set1-mediated heterochromatin assembly might involve Set1 methylating a nonhistone substrate similar to that of SUV39H1/Clr4 methylating Mlo3.
source: Set1-mediated heterochromatin assembly might involve Set1 methylating a nonhistone substrate similar to that of SUV39H1/Clr4 methylating Mlo3, an RNA processing and nuclear export factor that also contributes to RNAi-mediated heterochromatin assembly (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the H3K4me-independent function of Set1 and analogy to Clr4.

claim: The only known nonhistone target of Set1 is the kinetochore protein DAM1 in S. cerevisiae.
source: The only known nonhistone target of Set1 is the kinetochore protein DAM1 in S. cerevisiae (Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation.

claim: The S. pombe dam1 ortholog does not appear to be the target of Set1-mediated heterochromatic silencing.
source: However, the S. pombe dam1 ortholog does not appear to be the target of Set1-mediated heterochromatic silencing as repression of Tf2 retrotransposons and pericentromeric heterochromatin is maintained in dam1 mutant cells (Mikheyeva and Cam, unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by unpublished data.

claim: At developmental and stress-response loci such as ste11, Set1 may act in concert with transcription factors, including Atf1 together with Clr3 and other HDACs, to keep the target genes repressed in a steady-state condition.
source: At developmental and stress-response loci such as ste11, Set1 may act in concert with transcription factors, including Atf1 together with Clr3 and other HDACs, to keep the target genes repressed in a steady-state condition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Set1, Atf1, and Clr3 all contribute to repression of these genes.

claim: The chromatin states of developmental and stress-response loci probably support a transcriptionally poised Pol II that can rapidly upregulate transcription in response to appropriate environmental signals.
source: However, unlike heterochromatin, the chromatin states of these loci probably support a transcriptionally poised Pol II and in response to appropriate environmental signals enable Pol II to rapidly upregulate transcription.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known role of these genes in stress response and the presence of Set1 and Atf1 at their promoters.

claim: Null mutants of Set1C subunits were constructed using a kanamycin cassette.
source: Null mutants of Set1C subunits were constructed using a kanamycin cassette (Bahler et al., 1998; Mikheyeva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Double mutants were generated by standard genetic cross methods.
source: Double mutants were generated by standard genetic cross methods (Moreno et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Liquid cultures were grown at 30°C in standard rich media supplemented with 75 mg/l adenine (YEA).
source: Liquid cultures were grown at 30°C in standard rich media supplemented with 75 mg/l adenine (YEA).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The RNAi machinery contributes to the assembly of pericentromeric heterochromatin, in part by acting in cis to generate siRNAs.
source: The RNAi machinery is known to contribute to the assembly of pericentromeric heterochromatin, in part by acting in cis to generate siRNAs (Volpe et al., 2002; Noma et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Transcriptional activation of Atf1 is controlled by phosphorylation mediated by the stress-activated mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) Sty1 pathway.
source: The transcriptional activation of Atf1 is controlled by phosphorylation mediated by the stress-activated mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) Sty1 pathway (Shiozaki and Russell, 1996; Lawrence et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Ash2 and Sdc1 are thought to form heterodimers that together with Swd1 and Swd3 constitute the core of the Set1C complex.
source: For example, Ash2 and Sdc1 are thought to form heterodimers that together with Swd1 and Swd3 constitute the core of the Set1C complex (Roguev et al., 2001; Dehe et al., 2006; Southall et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations.

claim: S. pombe Set1 has been reported as a component of at least two complexes: a large ~1 MDa complex similar in size to that of S. cerevisiae Set1C and a smaller complex (~800 kDa) containing a shorter version of Set1.
source: Interestingly, S. pombe Set1 has been reported as a component of at least two complexes: a large ∼1 MDa complex similar in size to that of S. cerevisiae Set1C and a smaller complex (∼800 kDa) containing a shorter version of Set1 (Roguev et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation.

claim: Set1 localization at active and repressed targets was not hampered by the loss of H3K4me or its catalytic activity.
source: Set1 localization at active and repressed targets was not hampered by the loss of H3K4me or its catalytic activity.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP data comparing FLAG-set1, set1FH3K4me−, and set1-SETΔ in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inability of the set1FH3K4me− to methylate H3K4 appears to enhance its association with chromatin.
source: Indeed, the inability of the set1FH3K4me− to methylate H3K4 appears to enhance its association with chromatin.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 where set1FH3K4me− shows higher enrichment than FLAG-set1.

claim: Transcript abundance generally correlated with Pol II occupancy levels.
source: While transcript abundance generally correlated with Pol II occupancy levels (Figure 2C, middle panel) and 80% of promoter regions enriched for Set1 corresponded to actively transcribed genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), transcript abundance or Pol II occupancy levels did not linearly correlate with the levels of Set1 binding (Figure 2C, right panel).
evidence: This is shown by comparing RNA-seq and Pol II ChIP-seq data in Figure 2C.

claim: The repressed status of the ste11 gene was not noticeably affected by atf1Δ.
source: The repressed status of the ste11 gene was not noticeably affected by atf1Δ (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) and hence has little effect on the status of H3K4me3.
evidence: This is shown by expression analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Several repressed genes whose promoters are occupied by Atf1 exhibited increased H3K4me3 levels in atf1Δ cells.
source: However, we noticed that several repressed genes whose promoters are occupied by Atf1 exhibited increased H3K4me3 levels in atf1Δ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), probably owing to the loss of Atf1-mediated repression.
evidence: This is shown by ChIP-chip data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Defects in heterochromatic silencing result in transcriptional derepression of both the forward and reverse strands of pericentromeric repeats.
source: Defects in heterochromatic silencing result in transcriptional derepression of both the forward and reverse strands of pericentromeric repeats (Volpe et al., 2002; Moazed, 2011; Alper et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Heterochromatin assembly is characterized by the establishment of histone H3 lysine 9 methylation (H3K9me) and HP1/Swi6 proteins bound to H3K9me.
source: Heterochromatin assembly is characterized by the establishment of histone H3 lysine 9 methylation (H3K9me) and HP1/Swi6 proteins bound to H3K9me (Nakayama et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation.

claim: H3K9me/Swi6 is thought to provide a platform for the recruitment of histone modifiers such as HDACs which could restrict the accessibility of Pol II.
source: H3K9me/Swi6 is thought to provide a platform for the recruitment of histone modifiers such as HDACs which could restrict the accessibility of Pol II (Yamada et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation.

claim: Transcripts downregulated in set1Δ tended to be downregulated further in set1Δ clr3Δ.
source: Hierarchical clustering showed that transcripts downregulated in set1Δ tended to be downregulated further in set1Δ clr3Δ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and transcripts that were upregulated in set1Δ (i.e., Tf2s and subtelomeric regions) were further upregulated in the double mutants (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by hierarchical clustering and expression analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transcripts that were upregulated in set1Δ (i.e., Tf2s and subtelomeric regions) were further upregulated in the set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant.
source: Hierarchical clustering showed that transcripts downregulated in set1Δ tended to be downregulated further in set1Δ clr3Δ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and transcripts that were upregulated in set1Δ (i.e., Tf2s and subtelomeric regions) were further upregulated in the double mutants (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by hierarchical clustering and expression analysis in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Tor2-Mei2-Ste11 pathways are known to be activated during the meiotic development program.
source: Gene ontology analysis suggested that most of the upregulated transcripts in set1Δ clr3Δ are associated with stress-response processes that include the Tor2-Mei2-Ste11 pathways (Figure 5D; Figure 5—source data 1). These pathways are known to be activated during the meiotic development program (Otsubo and Yamamoto, 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citation.

claim: The set1Δ clr3Δ double mutant exhibited a synthetic slow-growth phenotype suggesting defects in chromosome segregation.
source: We observed that in contrast to wild-type or single set1Δ or clr3Δ mutant strains, a double mutant set1Δ clr3Δ strain exhibited a significant synthetic slow-growth phenotype and sensitivity to the tubulin inhibitor thiabendazole (Figure 4A), suggesting defects in chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the sensitivity to thiabendazole, a tubulin inhibitor that affects chromosome segregation.
